quote: Welches ist die kleinste Discriminante, zu der mehr als ein cubischer Körper gehört?
english: What is the smallest discriminant to which more than one cubic field belongs?
topic: The page completes an argument, based on Weierstrass's approximation theorem, that a function can be expanded as a series in an enumeration of polynomials with integer coefficients and constant coefficients; it then asks for the smallest discriminant shared by more than one cubic field and notes a plan to study Lambert's Beiträge zur Mathematik.

triage.modern_statement: Find the smallest absolute value |d| of a discriminant d for which there are at least two non-isomorphic cubic number fields K/Q with disc(K) = d. A quadratic field is determined by its discriminant, but a cubic field is not, so the question asks where this first fails. A modern way to see why it fails: for a fundamental discriminant D, the number of cubic fields of discriminant D is (3^r − 1)/2, where r is the 3-rank of the class group of Q(√D). Non-fundamental discriminants d = D·f² bring in ring class groups.
triage.answered_by: There is no single attributed solution, and I found no source that answers Hilbert's note directly. The answer comes from routine tables of cubic fields (Delone–Faddeev and Davenport–Heilbronn style enumerations, later Belabas's tables and the LMFDB). The smallest example is most likely |d| = 972, with the complex (one real embedding) cubic fields Q(∛6) and Q(∛12) = Q(∛18). Both have discriminant −27·6² = −972 by the standard pure-cubic formula, and they are not isomorphic. I worked out the −972 pair myself. I could not confirm that 972 is the smallest because I had no number-theory software and ran out of web searches. Among totally real fields, the smallest shared discriminant in the sources is 3969 = 63², which belongs to the two cyclic cubic fields of conductor 63.

evidence.claim: An arXiv paper confirms that two non-isomorphic cubic fields can have the same discriminant, and that this is studied as a known phenomenon.

A source names Q(∛6) as part of a pair of non-isomorphic cubic fields with discriminant 972 in absolute value. It pairs it with Q(∛2), but Q(∛2) has discriminant −108. The correct partner is Q(∛12) = Q(∛18), which has discriminant −972. This source is unreliable on the detail, and its arXiv number looks suspicious.
Lists of cyclic, totally real cubic fields give two distinct fields with discriminant 3969 = (3²·7)², so 3969 is shared by two totally real fields.
The smallest cubic field discriminant of all is −23, belonging to a single field (LMFDB 3.1.23.1). This is useful background when searching for the first repeated discriminant.
Background: Artin conjectured in 1928 about non-isomorphic cubic fields with the same discriminant, and the topic connects to 3-torsion in class groups of quadratic fields.

triage.why: This is a real but elementary question that finite computation settles. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Today it is answered by reading off cubic field tables such as the LMFDB. I checked by hand that Q(∛6) and Q(∛12) are non-isomorphic and both have discriminant −972, which gives a repeated discriminant with |d| = 972. One web source mentions the value 972 but pairs the wrong field with Q(∛6). I could not check against a full table that no smaller |d| repeats, which is why confidence is medium rather than high. The precise minimum is not a research topic. The broader area, how many cubic fields share a discriminant (3-torsion of class groups, Davenport–Heilbronn, Bhargava), is still active, but the sources here don't show anyone pursuing this specific question.
